doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

chapter: Buddy Rich, Sinatra and the Stones
title: Leaving Eastman for Buddy Rich
summary: Davis explains choosing Eastman for the Woody Herman pipeline, leaving three months before graduation for Buddy Rich, and his mother's reaction.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I can’t let this go by — I’m picturing you calling your mother saying, “Mom I’m leaving Eastman to go with Buddy Rich.” “Who’s Buddy Rich?” Did she know who Buddy Rich was?

She knew who Buddy Rich was, yeah, yeah. But yeah I mean the thing is I went to Eastman because they had a history of placing trombone players on Woody Herman’s band, especially like ten years before me, like for instance Jim Pugh and Birch Johnson and all these guys that I really looked up to and still do. And they were — it was kind of a pipeline there for a little bit so I thought well that’s the place that I should go. And as it turns out I ended up — I did play with Woody for a little bit but most of my big band time was with Buddy Rich. But it was a good pipeline and I knew when I got the call that this call might not happen again and I can always come back and finish my degree, which I did, and quite honestly a degree in trombone performance — an undergraduate degree in trombone performance is not very valuable in terms of the piece of paper. experience — extremely valuable. I mean it’s not like a music education degree where you can plug that into a work environment that you can get a job at. So it’s about — it’s like what we talked about at the beginning, the freelancing thing. It’s giving you the tools to be able to be a freelance musician. So I just thought this makes sense to me to take this. I understand it from my mom’s perspective. But she ended up being quite supportive about it so it all worked out in the end.
